2 Timothy — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

The first purpose of this letter appears to have been to tell Timothy what had happened during Paul's imprisonment and to ask him to come to Rome.

Paul was uncertain whether he would live to see Timothy again, so he also provided a wide range of counsel and encouragement to help him discharge his ministry faithfully.

Because this was a personal letter to one of Paul's closest friends, written amid the distress of imprisonment with death approaching, it offers a striking glimpse of the apostle's character.

It also gives compelling evidence that Paul sincerely believed the doctrines he preached.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesPaul expresses great affection for Timothy.1–5Exhorts him to improve his spiritual gifts.6–14Tells of many who basely deserted him; but speaks with affection of Onesiphorus.15–18
Paul thanks God for Timothy's faith (verses 1–5)

The promise of eternal life in Christ Jesus is the central message of ministers appointed according to God's will.

The blessings Paul asked for Timothy are the finest we can desire for those we love, including peace with God the Father and Jesus Christ our Lord.

All the credit for the good we do belongs to God.

True believers in every age share the same essential faith. Their faith is sincere and enduring, because it lives in them as an active principle.

The example of Lois and Eunice should encourage faithful women who teach children.

Some of the most helpful ministers Christ's church has known owe deep gratitude to God for the earliest impressions of faith made upon them by their mothers and other female relatives.

Stir up God's gift and guard the gospel (verses 6–14)

God has not given believers a spirit of cowardice or slavery to fear. He gives power, courage, resolution, love for him and a sound, peaceful mind.

When his strength supports us, we can bear affliction faithfully.

Whenever Paul spoke of Christ and redemption, he loved to dwell on them at length. Christ was all his salvation and should be all our desire.

The gospel's calling is holy and makes people holy. Salvation comes entirely by free grace, given in God's eternal purpose in Christ Jesus before the world began.

All the gifts God grants to fallen humans reach us through Christ alone.

The prospect of eternal happiness through him, the Resurrection and the Life, should move us to make our calling sure.

Those who remain faithful to the gospel need not be ashamed, though its opponents will eventually be ashamed.

Paul had entrusted his life, soul and eternal future to Jesus. Only Christ can preserve a soul through life, death and the last judgment.

A day is coming when everyone will be asked what they did with the soul entrusted to them. Did they serve sin or Christ?

The humblest genuine Christian stands upon the same foundation of hope as Paul: believing in Jesus and recognizing the saving change he has brought to the heart.

Timothy must hold firmly to the Holy Scriptures and the trustworthy pattern of gospel truth. Mere intellectual agreement is insufficient; we must love that truth.

The gospel is a precious deposit entrusted to believers. We must preserve it whole and pure, not through confidence in our own intelligence or heart but by the Holy Spirit living within us.

Remember faithful Onesiphorus (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.15-2Tim.1.18" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 15–18</reference>)

Many had shamefully deserted Paul. In contrast, Onesiphorus often encouraged and refreshed him through letters, counsel and comfort, without being ashamed of his imprisonment.

A good person seeks opportunities to do good.

Death and judgment are momentous realities. If we wish to receive mercy then, we must seek it from the Lord now.

For ourselves and our friends, the greatest request we can make is that we find mercy from God when we pass from time into eternity and stand before Christ's judgment seat.
classic_reading:
[2Tim.1.1-2Tim.1.5]
2 Timothy
The first design of this epistle seems to have been, to apprize Timothy of what had occurred during the imprisonment of the apostle, and to request him to come to Rome. But being uncertain whether he should be suffered to live to see him, Paul gives a variety of advices and encouragements, for the faithful discharge of his ministerial duties. As this was a private epistle written to St. Paul's most intimate friend, under the miseries of imprisonment, and in the near prospect of death, it shows the temper and character of the apostle, and contains convincing proofs that he sincerely believed the doctrines he preached.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
Paul expresses great affection for Timothy. | (1-5) |
Exhorts him to improve his spiritual gifts. | (6-14) |
Tells of many who basely deserted him; but speaks with affection of Onesiphorus. | (15-18) |
Verses 1-5
The promise of eternal life to believers in Christ Jesus, is the leading subject of ministers who are employed according to the will of God. The blessings here named, are the best we can ask for our beloved friends, that they may have peace with God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. Whatever good we do, God must have the glory. True believers have in every age the same religion as to substance. Their faith is unfeigned; it will stand the trial, and it dwells in them as a living principle. Thus pious women may take encouragement from the success of Lois and Eunice with Timothy, who proved so excellent and useful a minister. Some of the most worthy and valuable ministers the church of Christ has been favoured with, have had to bless God for early religious impressions made upon their minds by the teaching of their mothers or other female relatives.
[2Tim.1.6-2Tim.1.14]
Verses 6-14
God has not given us the spirit of fear, but the spirit of power, of courage and resolution, to meet difficulties and dangers; the spirit of love to him, which will carry us through opposition. And the spirit of a sound mind, quietness of mind. The Holy Spirit is not the author of a timid or cowardly disposition, or of slavish fears. We are likely to bear afflictions well, when we have strength and power from God to enable us to bear them. As is usual with Paul, when he mentions Christ and his redemption, he enlarges upon them; so full was he of that which is all our salvation, and ought to be all our desire. The call of the gospel is a holy call, making holy. Salvation is of free grace. This is said to be given us before the world began, that is, in the purpose of God from all eternity; in Christ Jesus, for all the gifts that come from God to sinful man, come in and through Christ Jesus alone. And as there is so clear a prospect of eternal happiness by faith in Him, who is the Resurrection and the Life, let us give more diligence in making his salvation sure to our souls. Those who cleave to the gospel, need not be ashamed, the cause will bear them out; but those who oppose it, shall be ashamed. The apostle had trusted his life, his soul, and eternal interests, to the Lord Jesus. No one else could deliver and secure his soul through the trials of life and death. There is a day coming, when our souls will be inquired after. Thou hadst a soul committed to thee; how was it employed? in the service of sin, or in the service of Christ? The hope of the lowest real Christian rests on the same foundation as that of the great apostle. He also has learned the value and the danger of his soul; he also has believed in Christ; and the change wrought in his soul, convinces the believer that the Lord Jesus will keep him to his heavenly kingdom. Paul exhorts Timothy to hold fast the Holy Scriptures, the substance of solid gospel truth in them. It is not enough to assent to the sound words, but we must love them. The Christian doctrine is a trust committed to us; it is of unspeakable value in itself, and will be of unspeakable advantage to us. It is committed to us, to be preserved pure and entire, yet we must not think to keep it by our own strength, but by the power of the Holy Spirit dwelling in us; and it will not be gained by those who trust in their own hearts, and lean to their own understandings. ( [2Tim.1.15-2Tim.1.18] 2Ti 1:15-18)
[2Tim.1.15-2Tim.1.18]
Verses 15-18
The apostle mentions the constancy of Onesiphorus; he oft refreshed him with his letters, and counsels, and comforts, and was not ashamed of him. A good man will seek to do good. The day of death and judgment is an awful day. And if we would have mercy then, we must seek for it now of the Lord. The best we can ask, for ourselves or our friends, is, that the Lord will grant that we and they may find mercy of the Lord, when called to pass out of time into eternity, and to appear before the judgment seat of Christ.

Serve faithfully as soldier, athlete and farmer (verses 1–7)

As trials increase, our faith, resolution and love for God and Christ should become stronger. That is not the same as relying on our own strength.

All Christians, and ministers especially, must remain loyal to Christ their Captain, determined to please him.

We must struggle against our sinful desires and corrupt habits, but we cannot expect a crown unless we compete according to the rules.

We must do good in the right way, lest our good actions themselves be spoken against. Even zeal for outward ceremonies or doubtful controversies can misdirect our energies.

The farmer must labor before receiving the harvest; the runner must run before receiving the prize. We must perform God's will patiently as we wait for what he promised.

Alongside prayer that God will give others understanding, we must encourage them to reflect carefully on what they hear and read.

Remember Jesus and endure (verses 8–13)

Suffering believers should look to Jesus, the Author and Perfecter of faith, who endured the cross and shame for the joy before him and now sits at God's right hand.

We should not be surprised when good people are treated badly.

Even when his servants are imprisoned, God's word cannot be bound.

Paul's suffering arose from his work for the gospel.

If we have died to this world's pleasures, profits and honors, we will live with Christ eternally in a better world.

Jesus is faithful both to his promises and to his warnings. The former secures believers' salvation; the latter makes unbelievers' condemnation certain.

Avoid quarrels and become a useful vessel (verses 14–21)

People eager to quarrel commonly dispute minor matters. Arguments over words can tear down God's work.

Some false teachers had not rejected the resurrection outright but distorted its meaning. Such error can overturn the temporary belief of some professing Christians.

The solid foundation has two assurances: God knows and preserves those who truly belong to him, and everyone who calls upon Christ must turn away from wrongdoing.

To enjoy the comfort of God's promises, we must seriously perform the duty that accompanies them. Christ gave himself to redeem us from every lawless deed (Titus 2:14).

The church is like a house containing vessels made from various materials, some for honorable service and others for common use.

When dishonorable vessels are removed, those God approves are prepared for his service. We must seek to be holy vessels, useful to the Master.

Correct opponents with meekness (verses 22–26)

The more earnestly we pursue what is good, the further we will move from evil.

Fellowship with faithful believers helps keep us separate from fruitless works of darkness.

The repeated warnings against religious quarrels show that true faith depends more on believing and doing what God commands than on intellectual cleverness in controversy.

A person who loves fighting and speaks fiercely is poorly equipped to teach.

Teaching rather than persecution is Scripture's method of addressing people in error.

Only God, who reveals the truth, can grant the repentance by which a person accepts it.

There is no uncertainty about his forgiving those who actually repent. What we cannot know is whether he will grant repentance to a particular person who currently opposes him.

Sin traps people in the devil's snare and makes them his captives. They cannot escape except through repentance as God's gift, which we should ask for in persistent prayer.
classic_reading:
[2Tim.2.1-2Tim.2.7]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
The apostle exhorts Timothy to persevere with diligence, like a soldier, a combatant, and a husbandman. | (1-7) |
Encouraging him by assurances of a happy end of his faithfulness. | (8-13) |
Warnings to shun vain babblings and dangerous errors. | (14-21) |
Charges to flee youthful lusts, and to minister with zeal against error, but with meekness of spirit. | (22-26) |
Verses 1-7
As our trials increase, we need to grow stronger in that which is good; our faith stronger, our resolution stronger, our love to God and Christ stronger. This is opposed to our being strong in our own strength. All Christians, but especially ministers, must be faithful to their Captain, and resolute in his cause. The great care of a Christian must be to please Christ. We are to strive to get the mastery of our lusts and corruptions, but we cannot expect the prize unless we observe the laws. We must take care that we do good in a right manner, that our good may not be spoken evil of. Some who are active, spend their zeal about outward forms and doubtful disputations. But those who strive lawfully shall be crowned at last. If we would partake the fruits, we must labour; if we would gain the prize, we must run the race. We must do the will of God, before we receive the promises, for which reason we have need of patience. Together with our prayers for others, that the Lord would give them understanding in all things, we must exhort and stir them up to consider what they hear or read.
[2Tim.2.8-2Tim.2.13]
Verses 8-13
Let suffering saints remember, and look to Jesus, the Author and Finisher of their faith, who for the joy that was set before him, endured the cross, despised the shame, and is now set down at the right hand of the throne of God. We must not think it strange if the best men meet with the worst treatment; but this is cheering, that the word of God is not bound. Here we see the real and true cause of the apostle's suffering trouble in, or for, the sake of the gospel. If we are dead to this world, its pleasures, profits, and honours, we shall be for ever with Christ in a better world. He is faithful to his threatenings, and faithful to his promises. This truth makes sure the unbeliever's condemnation, and the believer's salvation.
[2Tim.2.14-2Tim.2.21]
Verses 14-21
Those disposed to strive, commonly strive about matters of small moment. But strifes of words destroy the things of God. The apostle mentions some who erred. They did not deny the resurrection, but they corrupted that true doctrine. Yet nothing can be so foolish or erroneous, but it will overturn the temporary faith of some professors. This foundation has two writings on it. One speaks our comfort. None can overthrow the faith of any whom God hath chosen. The other speaks our duty. Those who would have the comfort of the privilege, must make conscience of the duty Christ gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, [Titus.2.14] Tit 2:14. The church of Christ is like a dwelling: some furniture is of great value; some of smaller value, and put to meaner uses. Some professors of religion are like vessels of wood and earth. When the vessels of dishonour are cast out to be destroyed, the others will be filled with all the fulness of God. We must see to it that we are holy vessels. Every one in the church whom God approves, will be devoted to his Master's service, and thus fitted for his use.
[2Tim.2.22-2Tim.2.26]
Verses 22-26
The more we follow that which is good, the faster and the further we shall flee from that which is evil. The keeping up the communion of saints, will take us from fellowship with unfruitful works of darkness. See how often the apostle cautions against disputes in religion; which surely shows that religion consists more in believing and practising what God requires, than in subtle disputes. Those are unapt to teach, who are apt to strive, and are fierce and froward. Teaching, not persecution, is the Scripture method of dealing with those in error. The same God who gives the discovery of the truth, by his grace brings us to acknowledge it, otherwise our hearts would continue to rebel against it. There is no "peradventure," in respect of God's pardoning those who do repent; but we cannot tell that he will give repentance to those who oppose his will. Sinners are taken in a snare, and in the worst snare, because it is the devil's; they are slaves to him. And if any long for deliverance, let them remember they never can escape, except by repentance, which is the gift of God; and we must ask it of him by earnest, persevering prayer.

Dangerous times and false religious appearance (verses 1–9)

Perilous times can arise even while the gospel is being preached. Persecution from outside the church is dangerous; corruption inside it is more dangerous still.

People increasingly gratify sinful desires instead of pleasing God and fulfilling their duties.

When everyone is eager to obtain more and anxiously protect possessions, people become dangerous to one another.

Those who do not fear God will not respect others. Children disobeying parents make life unstable.

Ingratitude for God's mercies feeds irreverence. We misuse God's gifts when we make them fuel for sinful passions.

Lack of natural affection in parents, unchecked temper and contempt for what is good also create perilous times.

God deserves our highest love, yet the sinful mind opposes him and prefers almost anything—especially bodily pleasure.

The appearance of godliness is entirely different from its power. Christians must distance themselves from people shown to be religious hypocrites.

Throughout the church's history, manipulative people have used flattery and pretended spirituality to gain the trust of the gullible and uninformed.

Their followers are always embracing new ideas but never seek the truth found in Jesus.

Like the Egyptian magicians, these deceivers resist truth with corrupt minds and lack genuine faith. Yet Satan and the spirit of error can mislead nations or churches only as far and as long as God permits.

Follow Paul's teaching and endurance (verses 10–13)

The more fully we understand Christ's doctrine as the apostles taught it, the more firmly we should hold to it.

When we know only part of the persecution believers suffer, we may be tempted to abandon their cause.

People may tolerate a merely formal profession of Christianity, while openly holding fast to Christ's truth and faithfully practicing godliness arouses the world's scorn.

By God's grace, faithful people grow in holiness. But through Satan's schemes and their own corrupt desires, wicked people grow worse.

The road of sin goes downhill: those who deceive others also deceive themselves. The history of the visible church sadly demonstrates the Holy Spirit's warning through Paul.

Remain in the God-breathed Scriptures (verses 14–17)

Anyone who seeks firm knowledge of God's ways must learn the Holy Scriptures, God's own revelation.

Childhood is especially suitable for learning. The greatest education children can receive begins with Scripture.

We must not leave the Bible neglected and scarcely ever opened.

The Bible is a trustworthy guide toward eternal life.

Prophets and apostles did not invent their message; they delivered what God gave them (2 Peter 1:21).

Scripture is profitable for every part of Christian living. Everyone needs instruction, correction and rebuke; the Bible addresses every situation.

If we loved our Bibles more deeply and remained closer to their teaching, we would benefit now and at last enjoy the happiness they promise through faith in Jesus Christ, the central subject of both Testaments.

The best defense against error is a solid knowledge of God's truthful word.

The greatest kindness to children is to teach them the Bible from an early age.
classic_reading:
[2Tim.3.1-2Tim.3.9]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The apostle foretells the rise of dangerous enemies to the gospel. | (1-9) |
Proposes his own example to Timothy. | (10-13) |
And exhorts him to continue in the doctrine he had learned from the Holy Scriptures. | (14-17) |
Verses 1-9
Even in gospel times there would be perilous times; on account of persecution from without, still more on account of corruptions within. Men love to gratify their own lusts, more than to please God and do their duty. When every man is eager for what he can get, and anxious to keep what he has, this makes men dangerous to one another. When men do not fear God, they will not regard man. When children are disobedient to their parents, that makes the times perilous. Men are unholy and without the fear of God, because unthankful for the mercies of God. We abuse God's gifts, if we make them the food and fuel of our lusts. Times are perilous also, when parents are without natural affection to children. And when men have no rule over their own spirits, but despise that which is good and to be honoured. God is to be loved above all; but a carnal mind, full of enmity against him, prefers any thing before him, especially carnal pleasure. A form of godliness is very different from the power; from such as are found to be hypocrites, real Christians must withdraw. Such persons have been found within the outward church, in every place, and at all times. There ever have been artful men, who, by pretences and flatteries, creep into the favour and confidence of those who are too easy of belief, ignorant, and fanciful. All must be ever learning to know the Lord; but these follow every new notion, yet never seek the truth as it is in Jesus. Like the Egyptian magicians, these were men of corrupt minds, prejudiced against the truth, and found to be quite without faith. Yet though the spirit of error may be let loose for a time, Satan can deceive the nations and the churches no further, and no longer, than God will permit.
[2Tim.3.10-2Tim.3.13]
Verses 10-13
The more fully we know the doctrine of Christ, as taught by the apostles, the more closely we shall cleave to it. When we know the afflictions of believers only in part, they tempt us to decline the cause for which they suffer. A form of godliness, a profession of Christian faith without a godly life, often is allowed to pass, while open profession of the truth as it is in Jesus, and resolute attention to the duties of godliness, stir up the scorn and enmity of the world. As good men, by the grace of God, grow better, so bad men, through the craft of Satan, and the power of their own corruptions, grow worse. The way of sin is down-hill; such go on from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived. Those who deceive others, deceive themselves, as they will find at last, to their cost. The history of the outward church, awfully shows that the apostle spake this as he was moved by the Holy Ghost.
[2Tim.3.14-2Tim.3.17]
Verses 14-17
Those who would learn the things of God, and be assured of them, must know the Holy Scriptures, for they are the Divine revelation. The age of children is the age to learn; and those who would get true learning, must get it out of the Scriptures. They must not lie by us neglected, seldom or never looked into. The Bible is a sure guide to eternal life. The prophets and apostles did not speak from themselves, but delivered what they received of God, [2Pet.1.21] 2Pe 1:21. It is profitable for all purposes of the Christian life. It is of use to all, for all need to be taught, corrected, and reproved. There is something in the Scriptures suitable for every case. Oh that we may love our Bibles more, and keep closer to them! then shall we find benefit, and at last gain the happiness therein promised by faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the main subject of both Testaments. We best oppose error by promoting a solid knowledge of the word of truth; and the greatest kindness we can do to children, is to make them early to know the Bible.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe apostle solemnly charges Timothy to be diligent, though many will not bear sound doctrine.1–5Enforces the charge from his own martyrdom, then at hand.6–8Desires him to come speedily.9–13He cautions, and complains of such as had deserted him; and expresses his faith as to his own preservation to the heavenly kingdom.14–18Friendly greetings and his usual blessing.19–22
Preach the word despite resistance (verses 1–5)

People may grow weary of Christ's plain gospel and prefer entertaining stories to clear, searching preaching.

They reject sermons that speak directly to their consciences and are relevant to their lives.

Those who truly care for human souls must remain watchful, accept the painful consequences of faithful ministry and use every opportunity to make the pure gospel known.

Paul's nearing death and his crown (verses 6–8)

The blood of Christian martyrs is not an atoning sacrifice. Yet their death can be an offering that acknowledges God's grace and truth.

For a good person, death is release from the prison of this world and departure to enjoy the world to come.

Paul had kept the faith and the gospel's doctrines, as both Christian and minister.

What comfort to be able to say this near the end of life!

The crown awaiting believers is a crown of righteousness purchased through Christ's righteousness. They have not yet received it, but it is securely reserved for them.

Believers may rejoice even amid poverty, pain, illness and death. But those who neglect the duties belonging to their calling weaken the evidence of their faith and may approach death troubled by uncertainty.

Come soon; bring books and necessary things (verses 9–13)

Love of the present world often causes people to abandon Christ's truth and ways.

Although Paul was guided by divine inspiration, he still wanted his books.

As long as we live, we still need to learn.

The apostles did not despise human means of meeting life's needs or of gaining further instruction.

Let us thank God for the writings of wise and faithful Christians from earlier generations, and use our reading so that our progress becomes evident to others.

Human supporters fail; the Lord does not (verses 14–18)

False brothers and sisters may be as dangerous as open enemies.

People willing to oppose someone like Paul deserve caution.

The Christians in Rome had eagerly greeted Paul when he arrived (Acts 28). But when standing with him appeared dangerous, they all deserted him.

Though God could justly hold their failure against them, Paul prayed for their forgiveness.

He was delivered from the lion's mouth, which Henry identifies as possibly Nero or one of his judges.

If the Lord stands beside us, he will strengthen us through trials and dangers. His presence more than compensates for the absence of everyone else.

Farewell and blessing (verses 19–22)

Nothing more is needed for true happiness than the Lord Jesus Christ present with our spirits. All spiritual blessings are united in him.

The finest prayer we can make for friends is that Christ will dwell with their spirits, make them holy, save them and eventually receive them to himself.

Many who believed as Paul did are already before God's throne praising their Lord. May we follow their example.
classic_reading:
[2Tim.4.1-2Tim.4.5]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
The apostle solemnly charges Timothy to be diligent, though many will not bear sound doctrine. | (1-5) |
Enforces the charge from his own martyrdom, then at hand. | (6-8) |
Desires him to come speedily. | (9-13) |
He cautions, and complains of such as had deserted him; and expresses his faith as to his own preservation to the heavenly kingdom. | (14-18) |
Friendly greetings and his usual blessing. | (19-22) |
Verses 1-5
People will turn away from the truth, they will grow weary of the plain gospel of Christ, they will be greedy of fables, and take pleasure in them. People do so when they will not endure that preaching which is searching, plain, and to the purpose. Those who love souls must be ever watchful, must venture and bear all the painful effects of their faithfulness, and take all opportunities of making known the pure gospel.
[2Tim.4.6-2Tim.4.8]
Verses 6-8
The blood of the martyrs, though not a sacrifice of atonement, yet was a sacrifice of acknowledgment to the grace of God and his truth. Death to a good man, is his release from the imprisonment of this world, and his departure to the enjoyments of another world. As a Christian, and a minister, Paul had kept the faith, kept the doctrines of the gospel. What comfort will it afford, to be able to speak in this manner toward the end of our days! The crown of believers is a crown of righteousness, purchased by the righteousness of Christ. Believers have it not at present, yet it is sure, for it is laid up for them. The believer, amidst poverty, pain, sickness, and the agonies of death, may rejoice; but if the duties of a man's place and station are neglected, his evidence of interest in Christ will be darkened, and uncertainty and distress may be expected to cloud and harass his last hours.
[2Tim.4.9-2Tim.4.13]
Verses 9-13
The love of this world, is often the cause of turning back from the truths and ways of Jesus Christ. Paul was guided by Divine inspiration, yet he would have his books. As long as we live, we must still learn. The apostles did not neglect human means, in seeking the necessaries of life, or their own instruction. Let us thank the Divine goodness in having given us so many writings of wise and pious men in all ages; and let us seek that by reading them our profiting may appear to all.
[2Tim.4.14-2Tim.4.18]
Verses 14-18
There is as much danger from false brethren, as from open enemies. It is dangerous having to do with those who would be enemies to such a man as Paul. The Christians at Rome were forward to meet him, Ac 28, but when there seemed to be a danger of suffering with him, then all forsook him. God might justly be angry with them, but he prays God to forgive them. The apostle was delivered out of the mouth of the lion, that is, of Nero, or some of his judges. If the Lord stands by us, he will strengthen us in difficulties and dangers, and his presence will more than supply every one's absence.
[2Tim.4.19-2Tim.4.22]
Verses 19-22
We need no more to make us happy, than to have the Lord Jesus Christ with our spirits; for in him all spiritual blessings are summed up. It is the best prayer we can offer for our friends, that the Lord Jesus Christ may be with their spirits, to sanctify and save them, and at last to receive them to himself. Many who believed as Paul, are now before the throne, giving glory to their Lord: may we be followers of them.
